lesson.title: The Loop Variable: Tracking Where You Are in a Repetition
lesson.summary: The loop variable is the name a for loop assigns to each item in a sequence as it iterates, giving the loop body a handle on whatever "the current one" happens to be.
lesson.body:
Every for loop names something. In the header for item in collection:, item is the loop variable: a regular variable that Python reassigns automatically at the start of every single pass through the loop. Before the first iteration, it is bound to the first element of the sequence. Before the second, it is rebound to the second element, and so on, until the sequence is fully exhausted. The loop body can then refer to that variable to work with "whichever item we're currently on," without you having to track its position by hand using a separate counter.

Naming a loop variable well makes code noticeably easier to read. Short names like i, j, and k are a long-standing convention for simple numeric counters, especially with range(), while more descriptive names pull their weight when the loop is walking over meaningful data, since fruit, student, or row communicates far more to a reader than a generic x would, especially in longer programs.

Watch the loop variable change across a real example:
scores = [72, 88, 91]
for score in scores:
    print("Grade:", score)
On the first pass, score is bound to 72, and the program prints "Grade: 72". On the second pass, score is rebound to 88, printing "Grade: 88". On the third pass, score is rebound to 91, printing "Grade: 91". Each reassignment happens automatically as part of the for loop's mechanics, driven entirely by position within the scores list, not by anything the body itself does.

One detail that surprises people coming from other languages: in Python, the loop variable does not disappear once the loop finishes. After this loop ends, score still exists and still holds 91, the last value it was assigned during the final pass. That can occasionally be useful for quick debugging, but relying on it as a design choice is usually a sign the logic belongs somewhere else, since a variable meant to represent "the current item during iteration" reads oddly once iteration is already over and the loop has moved on.

It is also worth knowing that reassigning the loop variable inside the body does not change what the loop does next. If you wrote score = 0 as the first line inside the body above, it would not skip the next item or restart the sequence from the beginning; Python has already queued up the next value from scores independently of whatever the body does to the name score in the meantime. The loop variable is simply how the current item gets exposed to your code, one pass at a time, which is exactly what makes a for loop's iteration usable rather than purely theoretical.

Sometimes a single loop variable is not enough, and Python's built-in enumerate() function addresses that by handing back two loop variables at once, an index and the item, as in for i, score in enumerate(scores):. That is still the same underlying idea, just with two names bound together on every pass instead of one, giving the body access to both position and value simultaneously without any extra bookkeeping.
